verdicts.note: Attacked on strength through the 2018 capital levy, and the attack fails. S7 (checked in the cache) gives only the $21 million amount, the 55-45 result and the projects (pool, roofs, ADA work). It gives no term, and no source calls the 2026 levy a replacement. The ballot title and explanatory statement do not use 'replace' or 'expiring' (S1, measure-7380.txt). A 2018 levy could not still be collecting in 2027 anyway: collections would have started in 2019 at the earliest, and a school capital levy runs six years at most. In March 2024 the board treated the 2018 levy as a past success ('something the district found success with in 2018') and needed a new way to pay for replacement Chromebooks and elementary cameras (S8). That means no capital or technology levy was paying for them then. There is also no offsetting bond payoff: the district 'does not have any bond debt' (S2). This differs from Spokane's Nine Mile Falls Prop 2, which was scored 1 because it took over an expiring bond's exact rate. Here $1.50 per $1,000 ($72.6M) is added on top of the 2025 EP&O renewal (S9), which fits the 'brand-new tax' tier, so 2. The basis's hedge ('if it were, that would argue for +1') is accurate but could be dropped. S1, S2, S3 and S7 support the basis; S8 would strengthen it. Spending was considered and rejected. Most items replace or upgrade existing assets (devices, bleachers, theater, grass fields to turf), and neither statement argues audit versus expansion. Parental-rights was also rejected: 'protect student information' is cybersecurity, not parents' access to records.

cost_line arithmetic checks out. 500 x $1.50 = $750 a year at the stated rate. The district's flyer shows '$63/month or $756/year' (S3, cache): $62.50 a month rounded up to $63, times 12, is $756. KDN reports $756 (S5), so '(the district rounds to $756)' is accurate. The yearly amounts $23,488,622 + $24,192,839 + $24,918,539 add up to exactly $72,600,000, and the rounded figures match S1. 'Not described as replacing an expiring levy' and 'alongside the district's EP&O levy' match S1, S2 and S9. what_it_does matches S2, S3 and S5 (2027-2029, simple majority, project list). pro_summary paraphrases measure-7380.txt accurately: state does not fund most repairs or technology, newest schools over 30 years old, dollars stay in South Kitsap for voter-approved projects, acting now prevents costlier failures. Katherine Ander and Carl Olson are the signers. Calling the committee 'South Kitsap School Supporters' follows its email domain in the pamphlet and S9. con_summary matches the Auditor's no-volunteer notice word for word. Optional: what_it_does leaves out parking, drop-off and school accessibility. Those are item (2) of the explanatory statement and are in the ballot title, so they could be added ('...bus radios, parking and accessibility at Burley Glenwood and East Port Orchard elementaries, student Chromebooks...').

Three accuracy fixes. pro_summary and con_summary match measure-7376.txt (signers, committee names, the study and stop-if-numbers-don't-work framing, rates below PSE's, shareholder dollars, local accountability; the 'broad, permanent authority', no second vote, Skagit/Island/Thurston, and 'has that authority now' points). Fixes: (1) cost_line says 'KPUD says property taxes and rates would not change because of the vote.' The fact publication (S3, cache) says 'Proposition 1 would not immediately change property taxes or electric rates', so dropping 'immediately' overstates KPUD's claim. (2) cost_line says Jefferson PUD 'paid $103 million ... in 2010'. The GM memo (S5, cache) says that in 2010 Jefferson PUD and PSE 'came to a purchase agreement of $103 million' and that Jefferson PUD took over operations in April 2013. PSE puts the cost at $109M (S8). (3) what_it_does says 'Puget Sound Energy serves the county today', but the dossier says PSE serves 'most of Kitsap County' (S7, S8). Corrected what_it_does: "Asks whether Kitsap Public Utility District (KPUD), now a water, wastewater and fiber utility, may build or buy electric generation, transmission or distribution facilities. Puget Sound Energy serves most of the county today. A yes vote gives KPUD that authority permanently with no second public vote required, though it does not have to use it. The board has committed to a feasibility study first, and if PSE will not sell, KPUD could seek to acquire the system through condemnation. A no vote ends the current effort." Corrected cost_line: "No tax, rate or bond in the ballot title. KPUD says the vote would not immediately change property taxes or electric rates. A yes vote does trigger the board's promised feasibility study, estimated at $300,000-$500,000. The cost of any later acquisition is unknown; Jefferson PUD agreed in 2010 to pay $103 million for PSE's much smaller Jefferson County system and took it over in 2013." Empty lean_mappings upheld. Taxes: the measure levies no tax and changes no rate (S1, S3). Spending is the closest call. The con side asks for restraint ('informed consent before expanding government authority'), and a yes vote leads to a $300,000-$500,000 study. But the ballot title authorizes no spending, both sides frame their vote as 'facts first', and putting yes on 'invest & expand' would require guessing what the board does later. Local-control: the pro side's 'local accountability' and 'local choice' point to pole_a, but a countywide PUD is itself a county-level authority (pole_b's 'county-level coordination'), and the change is from private to public ownership, not from a smaller unit to a larger one. Social and parental-rights do not apply. No missing mapping is proposed.
